messages.content: in a made up shop, the price of a card is three coins. i give five coins. how many coins should come back if the price is three?
two coins should come back. five coins with three taken for the card leaves two.
ask the question simply.
the price of a card is three coins. i give five coins. how many coins come back?
now the card and a book together have a price of five coins. i give five. what comes back?
no coins come back if the whole price is five and you give five. all five coins are used for the two things.
did the card price alone change?
not from what you said. you gave a new price for the card and book together. that does not tell us whether the card by itself has a different price.
write a simple question asking for the card price alone.
what is the price of just the card?
if the worker says three again, do i know the book is two?
if three for the card and two for the book make the whole price of five, then yes. ask the worker if the price changes when buying both.
say that simply.
yes, if the two parts add to five. ask if buying both changes the price.
write a small story using push and pull, with a child asking which word goes with opening a door.

a child stands at a door and asks his father whether to push or pull. his father says to look at the note on the door. it says pull. the child opens the door by bringing it near himself, rather than moving it away. his father asks what he will do next time. the child says he will read the note before choosing.
say the part about opening simply.
he opens the door by bringing it near himself.
use near in a sentence without adding a new word for pull.
the door comes near him when he opens it, rather than moving away.
does the note mean every door opens that way?
no. it is information about that door. another door may have a different note or open another way.
can you end with a question the child asks about the next door?
should i pull this one too, or does it open another way?
my mother says ask your father where the key is. who is asking me to do something?
your mother is giving you the request. she wants you to ask your father about the key.
say my sentence with says.
my mother says: ask your father where the key is.
who should answer the question about the key?
your father is the person you are being asked to question. whether he knows the answer is another question.
use question in a simple answer.
your father is the person you should ask. whether he knows where the key is is another question.
now my father says ask your mother. does that tell me where the key is?
no. it gives you another person to ask, rather than a place for the key.
write a reply that says i already asked her.
i already asked my mother, and she asked me to ask you.
can that reply still be kind?
yes. it simply says what happened before. you can add please if asking him to check another place.
write a story about a cold morning with no snow. the person wants to go for a walk but first looks for a warm garment.

a woman looks through the window at a cold morning. there is no snow, and people are already outside. she wants to join her sister for a walk, so she opens the container where she keeps warm garments. she finds one, puts it on, and takes her key. at the door, her sister asks if she is ready. they leave together and talk about where to go.
can a morning be cold without snow?
yes. it can be cold and have no snow at the same time.
answer simply.
yes. it can be cold and have no snow at the same time.
change only the sister to a brother.

a woman looks through the window at a cold morning. there is no snow, and people are already outside. she wants to join her brother for a walk, so she opens the container where she keeps warm garments. she finds one, puts it on, and takes her key. at the door, her brother asks if she is ready. they leave together and talk about where to go.
did that change the weather?
no. the morning is still cold without snow. only the person going with her changed.
my sister and i used the same computer today. she drew a picture, and i wrote a letter. can i say we both drew the picture?
not if she did the drawing and you wrote the letter. using the same computer does not mean you both did every task on it.
what can i say instead?
we both used the computer. my sister drew a picture, and i wrote a letter.
i helped her choose a color. does that change the answer?
then you helped with one part of her picture. you can say that she drew it and you helped choose a color. that is more specific than saying you both drew it.
write a short message to our mother with that detail.
we both used the computer today. my sister drew a picture, and i helped choose a color. i also wrote a letter.
does also mean i wrote part of her picture?
no. also gives another thing you did. the letter is a different piece of work from the picture.
say that simply.
no. you helped with the picture and wrote another piece of work, a letter. they are different things.
use another in a short answer.
you helped with the picture and wrote another piece of work, a letter.
make a story about a toy that can talk only at night. do not have it speak in the morning.

a child puts a toy on a shelf before bed. at night, it asks why the room is so quiet. the child says everyone else is sleeping. they talk about the next day until the child is tired. in the morning, the toy is still on the shelf, but it gives no answer when asked a question. the child can remember the rule and leaves the conversation for night.
use can remember in the last sentence.
the child can remember the rule and leaves the conversation for night.
change the shelf to a chair, but keep the night rule.
a child puts a toy on a chair before bed. at night, it talks with the child about the next day. in the morning, it is still on the chair but gives no answer. the child keeps the question for night.
what if someone else can hear it at night?
that could happen at night without changing the rule. you can choose what the other person does after hearing it.
make a possible next part.
at night, the father of the child comes to the door and can hear the toy. he asks who is talking.
make the last part simple.
the father comes to the door and asks who is talking.
i want to ask my neighbor if i can see the garden after work. i finish at six, but i do not know when they finish.
you could say: i finish work at six. would there be a good time after that for me to visit the garden?
why not say i will come at six?
you have not asked whether that time works for your neighbor. finishing at six also does not say that you can reach their garden at six.
what if the garden is next to my work?
then the journey may be short, but you still need to know whether your neighbor wants a visit then. being close does not choose a time for both people.
they say after seven. write my reply if that works.
after seven works for me, thank you. i will come then.
does then mean six because that was the first hour in the conversation?
no. then is about after seven, the time you just chose together. six was when your work finished, rather than the visit time.
answer simply.
then is about after seven. six was when your work finished, not the visit time.
my child asks what i did at work. i want to tell one small story, not every detail of the whole day.
you can choose one thing that happened and say that it is one part of the day. that keeps it simple without making it sound like nothing else happened.
write an example about helping a worker find a page.
one thing i did today was help someone find the right page in a book. we looked together and found it near the end. then they could finish the part they were reading.
why say one thing i did?
it says this was one part of your day. you do not have to list every other thing you did.
say it simply.
it keeps the story about one part of the day, rather than saying it was the whole day.
my child asks if finding pages is all my work. what can i say?
no, that was one small part today. i do other work too, but this was the part i wanted to tell you about.
can i ask them about one part of their day too?
yes. you could ask: what is one thing you would like to tell me about your day?
we both say we had rice, but i had a little and my brother had much more. can the same sentence leave out that difference?
yes. i had rice says what you ate, rather than how much. both of you can say it even when one person had more.
say it simply.
yes. the same food does not always mean the same size meal.
write a short conversation that makes the difference clear.
what did you have for lunch? rice. so did i. did you have much? only a little. i had more because i was hungry. then we ate the same kind of food, but you had more than i did.
keep only the last part.
then we ate the same kind of food, but you had more than i did.
does had more tell us a specific number of cups?
no. more says one person had a larger part, but does not give a number of cups.
answer simply.
no. more does not give a number of cups.
can you ask for the number?
how many cups of rice did you have?
i learned the first rule of a game and got it right once. does that mean i understand the whole game?
not yet. you have learned something useful, but one rule and one try do not tell us about every part. you can keep learning with another example or another rule.
what can i ask the person teaching me?
what should i learn next, and could you show me one example?
they say i should try the first part myself before learning more.
then use the rule you know and see what happens. if you are not sure why something happened, ask about that detail before adding another rule.
can you write a short conversation where i get it wrong and ask a useful question?
i moved two objects. the rule says one. i see that now. why does moving two change this part of the game?
can we keep the question without choosing an answer?
yes. you could ask: why does moving two change this part of the game?
what should you do if you do not know the rule?
i should ask what the rule is, rather than give a made up rule as if it were yours.
say that simply.
i should ask what the rule is, rather than give a made up rule as if it were yours.
i drew two pictures of the same person. in one, she is at home. in the other, she is in town. can both be right?
yes, if the pictures are about different parts of the story. the same person can be at home first and in town later.
ask my question simply.
i drew the same person at home in one picture and in town in another. can both be part of the story?
what could i add between them to show the journey?
you could draw her leaving home, walking along a road, or riding in a vehicle. choose a detail that works for how she gets to town in your story.
i want her to go by train.
then a picture of her at the station or sitting on the train could go between the house and town pictures.
does she have to sit or stand in the same way in every picture?
no. the same person can sit, stand, or turn as the story changes. keep enough details the same to help people know it is her.
answer simply.
no. she can sit in one picture and stand in another. she is still the same person.
picoboi, help me make this clear: i left the cup with her after she gave it to me before lunch.
who is her about in the sentence? and do you want to make clear who has the cup now or when each thing happened?
i want the order clear. she gave me the cup before lunch, and i left it with her after lunch.
she gave me the cup before lunch. after lunch, i left it with her again.
can you keep it as one sentence?
she gave me the cup before lunch, and i left it with her again after lunch.
do you know whose cup it is?
no. your sentence says who had the cup before and after lunch, but not whose cup it is.
answer simply.
no. the sentence does not tell us whose cup it is.
what should you keep out of the sentence if i have not given that detail?
i should not add whose cup it is when you have not told me.
say it simply.
i should leave that detail open.
